commentary: Aquinas reads Aristotle's opening claim - that all men by nature desire to know - as resting on three grounds. First, everything naturally seeks its own perfection, and the intellect's perfection lies precisely in knowing; so the desire to know is simply a thing's desire for its own completion. Second, understanding is the operation proper to man as man, distinguishing him from other creatures, and every nature takes a natural delight in its own proper activity. Third, all intellectual beings have some native longing for union with the higher, separate causes of things, and even our pleasure in mere sensation is a distant sign of that deeper appetite. Aquinas then works through Aristotle's ladder of cognition. Wholly stationary creatures have only the dimmest, most confused awareness. Animals with memory but no hearing, like the bee, display a kind of native skill but cannot be taught, since teaching requires the ability to receive another's words. Animals with memory and hearing together can be taught. Man alone rises further: from repeated memories of the same thing he forms experience, and from experience, by grasping the common cause behind many single cases, he forms art and science. Aquinas stresses that experience knows only that something is so in this or that individual, while art and science know the universal cause and can therefore explain why and can teach. Since wisdom is honored above all other knowledge, and its distinguishing mark is precisely the grasp of causes, wisdom must be understood as the science that knows things through their first and highest causes.

Aquinas draws together the marks people commonly attribute to a wise person - knowing everything in a general way, mastering what is difficult, teaching with precision, seeking knowledge for its own sake, and commanding rather than serving other studies - and argues that all of these converge on one science: the universal study of first causes. Because it treats the most universal principles, such a science implicitly contains knowledge of everything under them; because those principles are furthest from the senses, they are hardest to grasp; because it explains through causes, it alone truly teaches, since teaching is showing why, not merely that; and because it is desired for itself rather than for some further use, it is the freest and most honorable of the sciences, ordering the others as their end. Aquinas then follows Aristotle's account of philosophy's origin in wonder: humanity began by marveling at ordinary puzzles and advanced to greater ones, such as the motions of sun and moon and the origin of the universe, and pursued answers purely to escape ignorance, not for practical gain, which is confirmed by the fact that such inquiry only began once the necessities and comforts of life were already secured. Because this science is sought purely for itself, and because it either belongs to God alone or belongs to him most of all, it is the most divine of the sciences, both as the kind of knowledge most fitting for God to have and as knowledge concerning God as first principle. Aquinas notes that philosophy's proper end reverses its beginning: it starts in wonder at not knowing causes and terminates in the far better state of understanding them, so that wonder is dissolved rather than sustained.

Aquinas takes this chapter as Aristotle's formal introduction of the doctrine of the four causes, already treated in the Physics but now recalled as the framework for reviewing earlier thinkers. The formal cause is a thing's substance or essence, the answer to what it most fundamentally is; the material cause is what it is made from; the efficient cause is the source of change or motion; the final cause is the end or good for the sake of which something is or happens. Aquinas observes that the earliest philosophers, beginning with Thales, grasped only the material cause: they looked for some single underlying stuff - water, air, fire, or several elements together - that persists through all change, reasoning by analogy with how an individual like Socrates remains the same subject despite becoming musical or losing that quality. Because they fixed on this enduring substratum, they denied real generation and corruption of substances, treating all change as mere alteration of one abiding matter. Aquinas points out the deeper inadequacy Aristotle is building toward: a substratum cannot move or change itself, so something beyond matter is needed to explain why change occurs at all - the efficient cause. This is why the chapter ends by introducing Anaxagoras's mind, or reason, as the first tentative appeal to an ordering intelligence behind nature, which Aristotle praises, by comparison with his predecessors, as sounding like a sober man among the reckless. Aquinas treats this moment as the historical hinge where philosophy is pressed by the evidence itself toward recognizing a cause of motion distinct from matter.

Aquinas traces the further pressure that pushed early thinkers toward efficient causality. Once philosophers noticed order and beauty in nature, and not merely brute matter, some, following hints in Hesiod and Parmenides about love as a cosmic force, began to see that a principle uniting things is needed besides the material substratum. Empedocles goes further by positing two contrary efficient principles, friendship and strife, making friendship the cause of the good and orderly and strife the cause of corruption and disorder - and Aquinas credits him as the first, however dimly, to treat good and evil themselves as principles, since whatever causes good things is itself in some sense the good. Yet Aquinas follows Aristotle in judging that both Anaxagoras and Empedocles used their causes only fitfully rather than systematically: Anaxagoras invokes mind only when stuck, otherwise crediting chance causes, and Empedocles is inconsistent about whether love unites or separates things and whether strife does the reverse - like untrained fighters who land good blows without any real command of their art. Aquinas then turns to the atomists, Leucippus and Democritus, who reduced everything to the full and the void, treating fullness as being and void as non-being, and differentiated the atoms only by shape, arrangement, and position, comparable to how letters differ in form, order, and orientation. He notes that, like their predecessors, the atomists never seriously investigated the source of motion itself, leaving the question of what actually causes change unresolved even after multiplying material principles.

Aquinas explains that the Pythagoreans, trained in mathematics, mistook the principles of number - the odd and the even, corresponding to limit and the unlimited - for the principles of all reality, since they observed many likenesses between numerical ratios and things such as justice, soul, and the harmonies of music. Because number seemed to underlie everything, they treated numbers not as abstractions but as the very substance of things, and some among them arranged ten pairs of contraries, including limit and unlimited, odd and even, and good and bad, as the ultimate principles, even inventing a tenth heavenly body, the counter-earth, simply to preserve the perfection of the number ten. Aquinas treats this as an attempt to explain the world through formal, mathematical structure rather than matter, but faults it for confusing what is true only by abstraction and analogy with what is true of independently existing substances. He then turns to those who held that all reality is simply one being: Parmenides, Melissus, and Xenophanes. Aquinas distinguishes them carefully - Parmenides considers the one according to its intelligible nature or definition and so calls it finite, Melissus considers it according to extension in matter and so calls it infinite, while Xenophanes, the vaguest of the three, merely identified the one with God without clarifying which kind of unity he meant. Because a wholly immobile, undifferentiated one cannot generate anything, Aquinas judges that these thinkers, by denying motion altogether, actually abandoned natural philosophy, though Parmenides comes nearer the truth by also positing two subordinate principles, hot and cold, to account for the plurality evident to the senses.

Aquinas presents Plato as shaped early by the Heraclitean teaching, absorbed through Cratylus, that all sensible things are in constant flux and therefore cannot be objects of stable knowledge. From Socrates, who sought fixed universal definitions in ethical matters, Plato drew the further conclusion that if any true, stable definition is possible, its object cannot be the ever-changing things of sense; there must be separately existing realities corresponding to our universal concepts, which he called the Ideas or Forms, and sensible things are named after these and exist by imitating or participating in them. Between the Forms and sensible things Plato also placed the objects of mathematics, eternal and unchanging like the Forms but, unlike them, existing in many likenesses rather than uniquely. Aquinas explains Plato's account of the Forms' own principles: the Great-and-Small serves as their material element, a kind of indeterminate duality, while the One serves as their formal or essential principle, and Numbers arise as the Great-and-Small participates in the One. Aquinas notes that, on this analysis, Plato in the end recognizes only two of the four causes, the formal and the material - the Forms as the essence-cause of sensible things and the One as the essence-cause of the Forms themselves - while assigning the origin of good and evil to these same two elements, much as Empedocles and Anaxagoras had done. He also flags, as the root of Plato's error, the assumption that because the mind can consider a nature apart from its individuating material conditions, that nature must therefore also exist apart from matter in reality.

Aquinas treats this short chapter as Aristotle's summary judgment on the whole historical survey just completed. Reviewing every thinker considered, he finds that none named any cause outside the fourfold division already established, yet none named any cause with real clarity either. The material cause was recognized by nearly everyone, whether they supposed one principle or several, corporeal or otherwise. The efficient cause, the source of motion, was grasped only by a few, such as those who invoked love and strife or an ordering mind. The formal cause - the essence of things - was touched only obscurely by those committed to the Forms, since they made the Forms the essence of sensible things and the One the essence of the Forms, without ever properly distinguishing this from the other causes. The final cause, the end for the sake of which things exist and change, was acknowledged only incidentally: thinkers who called the One or being itself good treated goodness as somehow bound up with the first principle, but never actually claimed that things exist or come to be for the sake of that good, so that they spoke of the good as a cause without really meaning it as a cause in the proper sense. Aquinas draws the conclusion that this collective, if fragmentary, testimony of the ancients itself confirms the completeness and correctness of Aristotle's own division of causes into exactly these four, since no one, straining in every direction, ever discovered a fifth kind.

Aquinas now follows Aristotle's critical turn against the philosophers just surveyed. Against those who posited a single corporeal principle, he gives three charges: they ignore incorporeal realities, such as the soul, by admitting only bodily principles; they cannot consistently account for motion even though their own project of explaining generation and corruption requires it; and they never posit a formal cause, so they cannot say what a thing truly is, only what it is made from. He then shows that their own criteria for ranking the elements pull in opposite directions: judged by simplicity, the finest and most rarefied element, fire, should be first; judged by the order of generation, the densest and most compounded, earth, should be first, since composition follows simplicity in time. Aquinas resolves the tension by distinguishing what is prior in a particular process of coming-to-be, where potency precedes act in time, from what is prior absolutely, where act and perfection must come first - suggesting that only an incorporeal first principle could combine maximal simplicity with maximal perfection, which bodily elements cannot. Turning to Empedocles, Aquinas notes the added difficulties of elements generating one another despite being called first, of positing two independent contrary movers rather than one prior source, and of placing contraries like hot and cold in wholly separate subjects, which makes real alteration between them impossible. He treats Anaxagoras more sympathetically: read charitably, the claim that all things were originally mixed except mind gestures toward matter as pure indeterminate potency and mind as pure separate actuality, though taken literally it yields absurdities, such as qualities existing apart from any subject. The Pythagoreans, finally, are praised for reaching beyond sensible nature to mathematical principles, yet criticized because such abstract, unmoved objects cannot explain motion, generation, or the physical differences among bodies.

This chapter contains Aristotle's extended case against the Platonic Forms, and Aquinas organizes his defense along several lines. First, positing the Forms does not explain sensible things but merely doubles them, since for every kind of thing one now needs both the sensible instance and a separate Form of the same name - like someone unable to count a few things who tries to count by adding more. Second, none of the standard arguments for the Forms actually proves their existence: the argument from the sciences would generate Forms even of things nobody wants Forms of; the 'one over many' argument would yield Forms of mere negations; the argument that thought survives its object's destruction would give Forms even of perishable things. Third, and most fundamentally, Aquinas stresses that the Forms do nothing for the things they are supposed to explain. They cannot be the source of a sensible thing's motion or change, since they are themselves changeless; they are not needed for scientific knowledge, since the mind grasps universal natures through abstraction without requiring a separately existing counterpart; and calling sensible things 'copies' that 'participate in' or 'imitate' the Forms is, Aquinas notes, empty metaphor rather than genuine causal explanation, since one thing can resemble another without literally being modeled on it. Even the Phaedo's claim that the Forms cause both being and becoming fails, because something must still move a thing into existence at a given time, and the Forms, being immobile, cannot supply that efficient causality. Finally, where Plato identifies the Forms with numbers, further difficulties arise, since things identical in kind cannot be the cause of one another; and throughout, Aquinas underscores that by omitting efficient and final causality altogether, Plato reduces the natural, ever-changing world almost to the fixed status of mathematical objects.

Aquinas reads Aristotle's closing judgment as a summary verdict on the entire history just reviewed: the early philosophers, between them, touched on all four causes, but only obscurely and piecemeal, like children just learning to speak, who stammer and lisp before they can talk properly. As his example, Aristotle points to Empedocles, who came remarkably close to a genuine insight when he said that bone exists by virtue of a certain ratio, or proportion, among the elements mixed into it - which is really nothing other than bone's formal cause or essence, the answer to what bone most basically is. Yet Aquinas notes that Empedocles never followed this insight through: he did not consistently apply the same reasoning to flesh and the other bodily tissues, and he never clearly recognized that it is this formal proportion, and not simply the raw material elements he named, that truly accounts for why a thing is what it is. Aquinas treats this as emblematic of the whole tradition surveyed in the book: real intuitions of formal, efficient, and final causality appear here and there among the ancients, but always half-formed and never expressed with the clarity that Aristotle's own fourfold analysis achieves. The chapter, and with it the historical survey of Book One, closes by looking forward: Aristotle promises to return to the specific difficulties, or aporiai, raised by these earlier opinions later in the work, since working through such puzzles carefully will help advance the inquiry toward the truth about first causes and principles that the whole science of wisdom is seeking.
